note: The most cited general survey of the field, covering the GPT, LLaMA and PaLM families, training datasets, and evaluation metrics. A reasonable first read for anyone needing the shape of the field rather than a single result.
title: Large Language Models: A Survey
explain_beginner: Large language models like the systems behind ChatGPT multiplied so quickly that it became hard to keep track of how they worked or how they compared to one another. This paper does not run a new experiment. Instead it steps back and maps the whole field in one place, explaining how the major model families were built, what data they were trained on, and how researchers judge whether one model is actually better than another. It walks through the lineages behind well known systems such as GPT, LLaMA, and PaLM, describing what each family contributed and where it fell short. It also lays out the common ways models get tested, from simple accuracy scores to broader benchmark suites, and shows how leading models stack up against each other on shared tasks. The paper does not argue for a single new idea. Its value is as an orientation guide, giving newcomers a shared vocabulary and a sense of the landscape before they dive into any one narrower piece of research.
explain_business: This paper introduces no new capability, so it changes nothing about what an organization can build or buy today. Its practical use is as a map for people who need to choose between model families without becoming AI researchers first. Understanding that GPT, LLaMA, and PaLM descend from different design choices and training data helps a buyer ask sharper questions of a vendor, such as what a model was trained on, how it was evaluated, and which benchmarks actually resemble the buyer's own use case. The survey's comparison tables are a reasonable starting point for due diligence conversations, though they age quickly since new models ship constantly and the numbers here reflect only what existed at the time of writing. There is no cost, risk, or compliance finding to act on directly. The main business takeaway is procedural. treat any single benchmark score with caution, ask which evaluation methodology produced it, and expect today's leaderboard position to be temporary.
explain_practitioner: The paper is a structured literature review rather than an empirical study. It groups modern large language models by lineage, walking through the GPT, LLaMA, and PaLM families and summarizing the architectural choices, scale, and training recipes that define each generation. It then surveys the pretraining corpora, instruction tuning sets, and alignment data typically used to build these models, alongside the metrics and benchmark suites researchers rely on for evaluation, spanning knowledge tests, reasoning tasks, and generation quality. A comparison section places several prominent models side by side on shared tasks so readers can see relative strengths rather than take vendor claims at face value. The authors are explicit that a survey like this is a snapshot. Because the field moves fast, any fixed comparison table risks going stale within months as new models and benchmarks appear, and the paper's own coverage stops at the models and datasets known at the time of writing. It closes by naming open problems, including evaluation reliability and how far current benchmarks generalize.
